content: Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria and were conducted in Cameroon, India, Kenya, Malawi, South Africa, Uganda, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Zimbabwe. Among these, one was a randomized controlled trial, seven were cohort studies, four were cross-sectional studies, and one was a pre–post study. Five studies reported exclusive breastfeeding at six months, nine studies reported exclusive breastfeeding at three months, four studies reported early breastfeeding initiation within one hour of birth, and six studies reported breastfeeding initiation. The randomized controlled trial conducted in South Africa demonstrated improved exclusive breastfeeding rates at three months but did not show an improvement in early breastfeeding initiation rates. Four cohort studies (three of fair quality and one of poor quality) reported improved exclusive breastfeeding rates at three months following breastfeeding promotion interventions, with two of these improvements being statistically significant. Two low-quality observational studies reported higher exclusive breastfeeding rates at six months among women who received interventions, and a positive dose–response effect was observed between the number of intervention visits and exclusive breastfeeding rates. Evidence for breastfeeding initiation rates and early initiation is primarily supported by studies of low to very low quality. Six observational studies showed an increase in initiation rates post-intervention; however, none of these studies included comparison or control groups. The systematic review authors used the terms good, fair, and poor to assess the quality of the evidence. The review found that breastfeeding promotion and support positively influenced exclusive breastfeeding and breastfeeding initiation rates. The studies also indicated that the frequency of contact was associated with improved exclusive breastfeeding practices, with more frequent contacts leading to higher exclusive breastfeeding rates. Combinations of group education and individual counseling sessions on infant feeding, involving fathers and other family members, community health workers, and/or trained healthcare workers, as well as integrating programs for preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV with access to antiretroviral therapy (ART), positively affected exclusive breastfeeding. No studies reported on the effect of interventions on concurrent improvements in ART adherence, even though such interventions may have been similar in nature. No published studies were identified that provided evidence on promoting and supporting safe and adequate replacement feeding practices by mothers living with HIV. In the general population, interventions delivered across multiple settings (health systems, home and family environments, community environments, working environments, and policy environments) led to greater improvements in breastfeeding rates. The greatest improvements in early initiation of breastfeeding, exclusive breastfeeding, and continued breastfeeding rates were observed when counseling or education was provided concurrently in home and community settings, health systems and community settings, and health systems and home settings, respectively. Support for baby-friendly hospital interventions at the health system level was the most effective intervention in improving the rates of any breastfeeding. The authors concluded that improving breastfeeding rates requires delivering interventions across multiple settings by involving health systems, home and family environments, and the community environment concurrently. Indirect evidence from populations not affected by HIV demonstrates that exclusive breastfeeding rates and continued breastfeeding can be improved by interventions at the policy level, health facilities, and in communities. In general populations, the best outcomes are achieved when interventions are implemented concurrently through multiple channels. Cost–benefit studies were not identified. The values and preferences of representatives of national health authorities in 22 priority countries for the Global Plan (UNAIDS, 2011) regarding infant feeding were captured in a survey. The findings are included in the decision-making process and reported in Annex 3. Interventions to support improved and safer infant feeding practices are likely to be very acceptable to mothers living with HIV. A survey conducted among national health ministries before the guideline meeting found that health managers uniformly supported interventions to help mothers living with HIV feed their infants appropriately and safely. Health services already provide some support for infant feeding practices, both to the general population and to mothers living with HIV. However, investment in these aspects of program support is only very modest. The Guideline Development Group also considered that health authorities and individual health workers would be very supportive of individual mothers and linking with interventions taking place in communities, even if they were not initiated or coordinated by the health authorities. The investment required to improve health worker skills and competencies to support early initiation of, exclusive, and continued breastfeeding may be significant. Interventions, such as supervision, may also require significant resources to sustain them over time. However, the initial costs may be offset by long-term health benefits in the entire population, making them cost-effective. These costs need to be considered when health funds are allocated. Investment should be commensurate with the value of the intervention and health outcome: that is, major resources may be needed but would be fully justified. Breastfeeding is one of the few health behaviors that tends to be more frequently practiced among poorer communities than high-income populations. Interventions to support and improve feeding practices among mothers living with HIV are likely to improve feeding practices in the entire population and therefore reduce inequity. They are also likely to reduce the negative effects of spill-over messages, where mothers in the general population mistakenly adopt practices specific to mothers living with HIV. Improving feeding practices is likely to improve health outcomes most in the more vulnerable populations. Multiple analyses in non-HIV populations have shown that improved breastfeeding tends to improve health equity. In settings where maternal, newborn, and child health services promote and support breastfeeding and ART to increase HIV-free survival among infants born to mothers living with HIV, national and local health authorities should actively coordinate and implement services in health facilities and activities in workplaces, communities, and homes to protect, promote, and support breastfeeding among women living with HIV. Support for breastfeeding should be consistent across policies and programs, health facilities, and community activities for all women, including mothers living with HIV, to create an enabling environment for this practice. Support is needed not only at initiation and during the exclusive breastfeeding period but also to enable mothers to breastfeed for longer, that is, until 24 months or beyond. Therefore, this recommendation would have benefits across the whole population. The public health approach of national authorities promoting a single infant feeding practice among mothers living with HIV has resolved much of the confusion among health workers and communities regarding the choice of feeding practice. A recommendation to counsel and support breastfeeding should not be misunderstood as reverting to individual counseling about initial choice. Although there was no published evidence base regarding support for safer replacement feeding, additional support by skilled health workers can probably make replacement feeding practices safer. Long-term investment and sustained support for health workers at all levels are necessary to ensure continued capacity-building.
